frontmatter_description: Route here when spoken words are intended to convey an indirect request, warning, complaint, refusal, reminder, or invitation beyond their literal wording.
title: Indirect Language and Conversational Meaning
use_when: The speaker means something beyond the literal sentence, and the task is to infer the intended social meaning.
The utterance functions as a request, warning, complaint, refusal, reminder, invitation, or soft criticism rather than plain factual description.
The key question is what the listener is supposed to understand from the way it was said.
do_not_use_when: Do not use when the main issue is whether the statement is true or deceptive; route to lies, half-truths, or misdirection instead.
Do not use when the main issue is the speaker's hidden emotion rather than the communicative intent.
Do not use when the core task is audience adaptation, persuasion strategy, or choosing the best way to influence a listener.
Do not use when the scene is a straightforward literal statement with no implied social meaning.
decision_variable: what the speaker really wants the listener to understand
direct_route_rule: Route immediately when spoken words mean a request, warning, complaint, refusal, reminder, or invitation beyond literal text.
trigger_checklist: The literal words are incomplete, softened, or socially indirect.
The scene asks for the intended meaning, not the literal sentence meaning.
A request, warning, complaint, refusal, reminder, or invitation is being conveyed indirectly.
The listener must infer what is meant from context, tone, or shared expectations.
The utterance is not primarily about whether it is true or false.
workflow: Ask what social act the speaker is performing through that utterance.
Use context, relationship, and situational need to infer the intended meaning.
Prefer the indirect communicative function over the literal wording.
State the intended message in plain language.

special_case.title: Polite indirect request
special_case.rule: If a question or statement is phrased politely but clearly functions as a request, answer with the requested action or the intended request, not the literal sentence meaning.

worked_example.scene: A guest says, 'It is quite warm in here,' while looking at the closed window.
worked_example.question: What does the guest really want the host to understand?
worked_example.answer_logic: The literal sentence is about temperature, but the social meaning is a polite request to open the window or cool the room.

boundary_exit_rule: Exit to macro-08 if the central issue is truthfulness, deception, or selective disclosure.
Exit to macro-05 if the central issue is emotion inference from expression rather than communicative intent.
Exit to macro-09 if the central issue is how to persuade, advise, or adapt to the listener.
Exit to macro-04 if the carrier of meaning is a nonverbal cue rather than spoken words.
Add micro-34 when the literal meaning must be pinned down before the indirect meaning is read.
Add micro-35 when the utterance functions as a request, warning, refusal, or invitation in disguise.
Add micro-36 when context-driven implicature must be computed.
Add micro-39 when the puzzle is why the speaker phrased it indirectly (motive).
Add micro-48 when the indirect wording protects a private or sensitive disclosure.

references.route_signal: A speaker says one thing but clearly intends the listener to infer a different social action or practical meaning.
hard_boundary: Not about whether the utterance is factually true.
Not about hidden feeling unless the feeling is only a clue to the intended message.
Not about optimizing persuasion strategy or audience calibration.
Not about nested belief or false-belief reasoning unless needed only as context.
shortcut_to_avoid: Do not overcall this macro for any nonliteral sentence; some nonliteral cases are lies, sarcasm with truth-status questions, or persuasion problems.
Do not answer from literal semantics alone when the scene clearly signals an intended social meaning.
Do not confuse indirectness with emotional concealment.
common_failure_modes: Answering the literal sentence instead of the intended meaning.
Routing sarcasm or irony to emotion when the task is really conversational meaning.
Routing a deceptive statement here when the core is truth value or misleading effect.
Treating a polite request as a factual comment.

minimal_pair.case: A person says, 'Can you pass the salt?' at dinner.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: The literal form is a question about ability, but the intended meaning is a request.

minimal_pair.case: A person says, 'I already finished my part,' while in fact they only completed half and want the listener to think it is fully done.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: This is a near miss: the wording is selected to create a false impression of the facts, so truth status is the central issue and it routes to macro-08 instead.

boundary_stress_test: If the utterance is indirect but the question asks whether it is true, shift to lies or misdirection.
If the utterance is indirect but the main challenge is tailoring it to the listener, shift to persuasion or advice.
If the utterance hides feeling without changing the social act, shift to hidden emotion.
If the utterance is a live misunderstanding that needs repair, this macro can still be used for the meaning inference, but the repair macro may become the better direct route.
references.generalization_note: Use this macro as the reusable prototype for indirect speech acts across requests, warnings, complaints, refusals, reminders, invitations, and soft criticism; micro ids are only for diagnosis, repair, and boundary explanation.

validation_seed.positive_pattern: The speaker uses literal words that clearly function as a request, warning, complaint, refusal, reminder, or invitation in context.
validation_seed.near_miss_pattern: The utterance is partly misleading or selectively true, so the main issue is truth status rather than indirect meaning.
validation_seed.boundary_pattern: The utterance is socially indirect, but the key task is to adapt the message to the listener's beliefs, motives, or expertise.

notes: This macro is a direct scene prototype, not just a bundle of micro skills.
Use the micro expansions only when needed for finer diagnosis or explanation.
Keep the answer centered on intended conversational meaning rather than literal wording.
core_question: what the speaker really wants the listener to understand
